text: Unless a Dockerfile says otherwise, the process inside your container starts as root. That's convenient in development — nothing blocks a file write, nothing blocks binding a port — but container isolation isn't a hypervisor-grade boundary. If there's ever a container-escape bug or a bad mount, it's far more dangerous when the process that found it was already running as root.

Least privilege applies inside the container exactly like it applies everywhere else. A Dockerfile can create a dedicated, unprivileged user and group, grant that user ownership of only the directories it needs, and switch to it before the application ever runs — giving the process just enough access to do its job and nothing more.

In practice that's groupadd and useradd to create the account, chown on copy to set ownership, and a USER line before the final CMD. That USER instruction is the one that matters — everything after it, including the command that actually runs your app, executes as that unprivileged user instead of root.

Kubernetes expresses the same idea in a pod's security context. runAsNonRoot set to true doesn't just document intent — it makes the kubelet refuse to start the pod at all if the image would actually run as root, catching a Dockerfile mistake before it ever reaches a cluster.

Beyond the user, a read-only root filesystem with a small tmpfs scratch mount stops anything from modifying files at runtime. And root itself isn't one switch — it's a bundle of Linux capabilities, so dropping all of them and re-adding only what's genuinely needed, like binding a privileged port, narrows what a compromised process can do even further.

None of these controls are exotic on their own — a dedicated user, a read-only filesystem, a trimmed capability set — but stacked together they turn a compromised container from a useful foothold into a dead end for an attacker.
